title: Metamodernism
thinkers: David Foster Wallace (forerunner of the "New Sincerity")
keyWorks: D. F. Wallace, "E Unibus Pluram: Television and U.S. Fiction" (1993)
T. Vermeulen, R. van den Akker, "Notes on Metamodernism" (2010)
Metamodernism: Historicity, Affect, and Depth after Postmodernism (edited volume, 2017)
summary: Metamodernism is a concept proposed in 2010 by the Dutch cultural theorists Timotheus Vermeulen and Robin van den Akker to describe the "structure of feeling" of our time. It is not a philosophical school in the strict sense but a way of understanding how, after postmodern irony, people are once again daring to be sincere, to hope, and to reach for big meanings — without forgetting their doubts. Metamodernism's central image is oscillation: a swinging back and forth between opposites.
onEmotions: For metamodernism, feelings are not something to be embarrassed about or to hide behind irony. A "structure of feeling" (a phrase coined by the cultural critic Raymond Williams) is the shared emotional climate of an era, and today, Vermeulen and van den Akker suggest, it oscillates between enthusiasm and skepticism, hope and melancholy. The metamodern person can know that their feelings are "naive" and still live them seriously — this is called "informed naivety." Contradictory feelings here are not a mistake but a normal state: you can laugh and cry at once, believe and doubt at once.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is often born from being pulled in different directions at the same time. Metamodernism describes this state as a feature of our era: Vermeulen and van den Akker speak of "oscillation" — a swinging between opposite poles, such as hope and doubt, engagement and detachment. From their point of view, there is no need to forcibly stop this swinging by choosing one side forever. They use the Greek word "metaxy" — "in-betweenness," the state of being "between." Seen this way, anxiety is not a breakdown but a sign that you are living in the tension between two things that matter to you. You might try not to win this inner argument right away, but to sway gently between the poles like a pendulum — and notice that there is a kind of steadiness in motion too.
anxiety.practice: Name the two poles you are swinging between right now. Write them at opposite edges of a sheet of paper and put a dot where you are at this moment.

fear.text: Fear can be the fear of taking a step that might not work out. Metamodernism offers an interesting answer, drawing on Kant: act "as if" — as if the goal were achievable, even knowing there are no guarantees. Vermeulen and van den Akker describe this as a movement that does not wait for certainty of success. This is not recklessness, nor a naive belief that all will be well. It is "informed naivety": you understand the risks, you can see it might not work out — and you still choose to try, because the path itself has meaning. From this point of view, fear does not have to be fully conquered before you move. It can walk beside you, like a sober companion, while you take a small step "as if."
fear.practice: What small step could you take "as if" everything were going to work out? Write it down without promising yourself any result.

quote.text: Metamodernism moves for the sake of moving, attempts in spite of its inevitable failure; it seeks forever for a truth that it never expects to find.
quote.author: Timotheus Vermeulen, Robin van den Akker

sadness.text: Sadness doesn't need to justify itself. Metamodernism seems to understand it especially well: Vermeulen and van den Akker name melancholy as one of the poles between which the feeling of our time oscillates — alongside hope. Scholars of metamodernism find this combination throughout contemporary culture: in films and songs where a bright, almost childlike naivety sits next to a quiet sorrow. Postmodernism often hid sadness behind irony — "oh well, none of this is serious." The metamodern sensibility allows you to be sad in earnest without losing your capacity for lightness. From this point of view, sadness is not the opposite of hope but its neighbor. You can let it be, knowing the pendulum will swing the other way too — not because you force it, but because that is how a living feeling works.
sadness.practice: Think of a song or film in which sadness and tenderness sound together. Stay with that combination for a minute.

grief.text: Grief is a feeling with no room for irony, and rightly so. Metamodernism arose in large part as a reaction to weariness with postmodern detachment, when it was customary to speak of the most important things with a smirk. Loss breaks through that defense: in the face of it, you cannot "pretend." From a metamodern point of view, one could say that grief brings us back to the "New Sincerity" — a readiness to speak plainly and feel in earnest, even if it looks vulnerable. At the same time, metamodernism does not ask you to choose a single state: in grief, tears can sit beside unexpected laughter over a shared memory, pain beside gratitude. This swinging is not a betrayal of the loss. It is a sign that you are alive and that you love, and you can accept it without judgment.
grief.practice: Recall one detail about what you have lost that brings you both pain and a smile. Let both feelings sit side by side.

loneliness.text: Loneliness can feel especially sharp in a world where everyone seems to be constantly connected. Metamodernism describes an era grown tired of ironic watching from the sidelines. The writer David Foster Wallace, often seen as a forerunner of the "New Sincerity," observed that irony is good for exposing things but nearly useless for building anything. It is hard to truly meet someone from behind it. From this point of view, part of loneliness may come from a habit of keeping your distance, of always being "a little above" your own feelings. The metamodern answer is "informed naivety": risking saying plainly "I'm lonely" or "I miss you," knowing it may sound awkward. Sincerity is vulnerable, but it is exactly what opens the door through which another person can come in.
loneliness.practice: Write one sincere message to someone you miss — with no joke at the end. You don't have to send it.

anger.text: Anger can be an honest response to something that matters to you. Postmodern culture often taught us to meet injustice with an ironic shrug: "well, that's how the world is." Metamodernism describes a return of seriousness and of what Vermeulen and van den Akker call "pragmatic idealism": the wish to change something, together with a sober understanding that the result will not be ideal. From this point of view, anger is not something to mock or hide. It can become the energy of idealism. But metamodernism also offers oscillation: between hot engagement and a step back, between conviction and doubt about being right. You can let your anger sound at full strength and still leave a small window open inside for the question: "What if I'm not seeing everything?"
anger.practice: Write down what makes you angry, and below it one sentence that begins with "And yet, perhaps…".

shame.text: Shame is often tied to the fear of seeming ridiculous, naive, "too much." Postmodernism made irony the main defense: if you say everything with a smirk, no one can catch you having a sincere feeling. Metamodernism describes a turn in which this defense stops working and starts to feel cramped. As early as 1993, David Foster Wallace suggested that the new rebels would be those who dared to step back from irony and seriously stand up for simple values, at the risk of looking sentimental. From this point of view, shame about "too strong" feelings is largely an echo of a cultural norm, not the truth about you. You might try "informed naivety": admit that you know how it looks from outside — and still stay with your feeling.
shame.practice: Name one feeling or passion you are embarrassed about as "naive." Say to yourself: "Yes, it's naive — and it's mine."

quote.text: The next real literary "rebels" in this country might well emerge as some weird bunch of anti-rebels, born oglers who dare somehow to back away from ironic watching, who have the childish gall actually to endorse and instantiate single-entendre principles.
quote.author: David Foster Wallace
quote.source: "E Unibus Pluram: Television and U.S. Fiction" (1993)

guilt.text: Guilt is a sign that your actions and other people matter to you. Metamodernism doesn't write about guilt directly, but in the light of its ideas one could say this. Postmodern culture sometimes taught us to dissolve guilt with irony: "everyone lives like this," "nothing matters." The metamodern sensibility, by contrast, gives actions their weight back — while remembering imperfection. "Pragmatic idealism" means striving to act well while knowing in advance that you won't be perfect. In this light, guilt is not proof that you are a bad person but a moment of oscillation between the ideal and reality. You can acknowledge a mistake seriously, do what is within your power, and then let the pendulum swing back — toward accepting yourself as imperfect but trying.
guilt.practice: Write two lines: "What I wanted to do" and "What I managed to do." Look at the distance between them without passing sentence.

envy.text: Envy is unpleasant, but it honestly shows you what you want. In postmodern culture it was often customary to hide desires behind irony: to pretend you "don't care," that you're above it. From a metamodern point of view, one could say that envy is a desire that was denied the right to sincerity. Metamodernism offers the "New Sincerity": admit your desire plainly, without the self-irony that devalues it. And at the same time stay clear-eyed, remembering that you only see part of someone else's life. This swinging between "I really want this" and "I don't know the whole picture" makes envy less corrosive. It becomes a hint: what you truly value — and what small step toward it is possible without comparison.
envy.practice: Finish this sincerely, without irony: "I want…". Read the sentence aloud and notice what you felt.

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy can feel like a state in which nothing touches you. Metamodernism grew in large part out of an awareness of this kind of emptiness at the end of the 20th century. Postmodernism taught culture to see that any big meaning could be taken apart, exposed and mocked — and many people felt that nothing was left underneath. Vermeulen and van den Akker describe the new generation's answer: not a return to naive faith, but building meaning anew — they speak of "reconstruction" instead of endless deconstruction — while understanding that there may be no final answer. From this point of view, emptiness is not the last word about the world but a pause between meanings taken apart and meanings not yet put together. You don't have to rush it, but you can leave the door ajar.
emptiness.practice: Recall something that once seemed important to you and then lost its value. Is there even one tiny part of it you'd like to keep?

confusion.text: Confusion is a natural reaction to a time with no single shared answer. Metamodernism describes an era in which the old grand narratives of progress have weakened, while pure irony has also stopped comforting us. Vermeulen and van den Akker propose accepting this state not as chaos but as oscillation — a swinging between opposites that never comes to a final stop. For them, this is not weakness but a form of living thought: the culture of our time believes and doubts at once, builds and dismantles at once. From this point of view, confusion is not a sign that you've missed something but an honest reflection of the era. You can allow yourself not to make a final choice yet, and keep moving even as you waver.
confusion.practice: Write: "On the one hand… On the other hand…" — and don't put a full stop at the end. Let both sides be true for now.

quote.text: Metamodernism oscillates between a modern enthusiasm and a postmodern irony, between hope and melancholy, between naïveté and knowingness, empathy and apathy, unity and plurality, totality and fragmentation, purity and ambiguity.
quote.author: Timotheus Vermeulen, Robin van den Akker

fatigue.text: Fatigue can come from work, and it can also come from constantly having to stay on the defensive. From a metamodern point of view, you might notice a particular fatigue of our time — fatigue from irony. When everything has to be devalued with a joke, when nothing can be loved openly and nothing invested in seriously, it takes enormous hidden effort. David Foster Wallace wrote that irony, once it becomes the norm, turns from a liberation into a tyranny. Metamodernism suggests not trading irony for heroic enthusiasm — that is exhausting too — but allowing yourself to swing between engagement and rest. A pendulum has a moment when it pauses at the far end of its arc. Your fatigue may be that moment — not a defeat, but a natural part of the motion.
fatigue.practice: Find one area where you're tired of "keeping a straight face." Let yourself stop doing it for five minutes.

boredom.text: Boredom can seem like a sign that the world is used up and everything has been done before. This is a very postmodern feeling: everything is a quotation, everything a repeat. Metamodernism answers it with a turn toward what Vermeulen and van den Akker call neo-romanticism. They recall the German Romantic Novalis, who proposed giving the ordinary a mysterious aspect. This is not denying that the world is full of repetition, but a conscious decision to look at the familiar as if something greater were hidden in it — that very "informed naivety." From this point of view, boredom is an invitation to a small experiment: to treat a familiar thing seriously and with wonder, even while knowing it's a bit of a game.
boredom.practice: Pick a familiar object or route and describe it in two sentences the way you would describe something magical.

quote.text: The world must be romanticized. […] Insofar as I present the commonplace with higher meaning, the customary with a mysterious appearance, the known with the dignity of the unknown, the finite with an infinite appearance, I romanticize it.
quote.author: Novalis

joy.text: In metamodernism, joy is rehabilitated. Postmodern culture often regarded open joy with suspicion: delight seemed naive, enthusiasm a little ridiculous. Metamodernism describes the return of what Vermeulen and van den Akker call modern enthusiasm — but now without the illusion that happiness will be eternal and unclouded. This is joy with open eyes: you know about the world's troubles and still allow yourself to rejoice. Such "informed naivety" is not foolish but brave. From this point of view, joy doesn't need to be justified or devalued with a joke — you can simply live it. And if the pendulum later swings toward sadness, that won't cancel the fact that the joy was real.
joy.practice: Tell yourself about your joy in one sentence — with no "but" and no irony at the end.

love.text: Love and tenderness are perhaps the main territory of the "New Sincerity." Postmodern irony taught us to speak of love in quotation marks, as if a plain "I love you" were a cliché too awkward to say. Metamodernism describes a culture that once again dares to use that cliché, knowing it is a cliché — and says it in earnest anyway. That is "informed naivety": remembering the whole history of words about love and choosing them all the same. From this point of view, tenderness doesn't require originality. It can be expressed through simple, even banal gestures — and they will be real because you put yourself into them. To love in the metamodern sense is to risk looking sentimental for the sake of genuine closeness.
love.practice: Choose the simplest, most "banal" phrase of tenderness and say or write it to someone you love — in earnest.

gratitude.text: Gratitude is hard to express ironically without it getting lost. From a metamodern point of view, one could say that gratitude is one of the purest forms of the "New Sincerity": to say "thank you" in earnest is to admit that you depend on others and that there's nothing wrong with that. Postmodern culture was often embarrassed by such simplicity. The metamodern sensibility, as Vermeulen and van den Akker describe it, reaches toward restoring meaning where it has been taken apart — toward "reconstruction" instead of endless deconstruction. Gratitude is just such a small reconstruction: out of scattered events, you assemble a coherent story of what you have been given. You can allow yourself to give thanks directly, without self-irony, even if it seems a little old-fashioned.
gratitude.practice: Write three lines: who gave you what, and when — without caveats or jokes, simply as a fact.

hope.text: Hope is the central feeling of metamodernism, but hope of a particular kind. Vermeulen and van den Akker describe it through Kant: we act "as if" the world could move toward the better, though we have no proof that it will. This is neither the naive optimism of modernity, which believed in inevitable progress, nor postmodern skepticism, which declared all hope an illusion. It is a hope that knows its own fragility and chooses to exist anyway. They speak of hope and melancholy as two poles of a single movement. From this point of view, you can hope without promising yourself a result and without being ashamed of your doubts. Hope here is not a forecast but a way of keeping your direction as you walk.
hope.practice: Write down what you hope for, starting with the words "As if…". Notice how the feeling changes.

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is one of the most characteristic feelings of our time, and metamodernism treats it with understanding. Scholars of metamodernism note that the culture of recent years is full of longing for the past: vintage things, film photography, remakes of old stories. Postmodernism treated the past as a set of quotations for ironic play. The metamodern attitude is different: the past once again becomes a source of sincere feeling, even though we know it cannot be brought back and that it was not ideal. This is nostalgia with open eyes — a swinging between tenderness for what is gone and a sober understanding of its limits. From this point of view, you can allow yourself to miss the past without turning it into a myth and without being ashamed of your attachment.
nostalgia.practice: Name what you miss and finish the sentence: "It wasn't perfect, and still, what's dear to me is…".

craving.text: A sharp craving — "I want it right now" — can be very strong, and there's nothing shameful in that. David Foster Wallace, considered a forerunner of the metamodern "New Sincerity," speaks in his famous speech "This Is Water" about our "default setting" — automatic reactions that switch on by themselves. His thought is that real freedom is not the absence of desires but the ability, at least sometimes, to choose what to pay attention to. From this point of view, one could say that a craving is a default setting announcing itself loudly. You don't need to defeat it once and for all. You can simply notice: "there it is" — and with that small noticing, already step a little out of autopilot.
craving.practice: When a craving rises, say to yourself: "This is the default setting." Then shift your attention to one thing near you — a sound, your breath, the feeling in your palms — for at least a minute.

addiction.text: Addiction is not a moral failure but a circle that is genuinely hard to get out of. David Foster Wallace's novel Infinite Jest is in large part about addiction and about people trying to get free of it. Wallace portrays mutual-help groups with great respect: their simple slogans like "one day at a time" seem banal to the ironic mind, but, as the characters notice, they somehow work if you say them in earnest. This is a very metamodern thought: you don't have to fully believe or understand everything in order to try sincerely. From this point of view, getting out of the circle is not a heroic leap but a willingness to do simple things again and again, irony set aside, together with others.
addiction.practice: Choose one simple phrase of support that seems a little banal to you and say it to yourself today in earnest. If you like, you could drop in on a mutual-help group such as AA or NA — just to listen.

hangover.text: The morning after can be hard: your body aches, and anxiety, shame and gaps in memory come too. That's understandable and doesn't make you any worse a person. From a metamodern point of view, you might notice that a hangover is a sharp swing: yesterday everything was easy and a little ironic, today it's serious and heavy. Metamodernism describes such swings as the ordinary rhythm of our time, not as a breakdown. It suggests not choosing one extreme — neither "no big deal, forget it" nor "I'm a terrible person." You can hold both sides: yes, it was fun, and yes, right now it's bad. "Informed naivety" lets you honestly acknowledge what happened and still treat yourself with warmth rather than a verdict.
hangover.practice: Write two lines: "What really happened yesterday" and "How I can take care of myself today." Answer briefly and without judgment.

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria can be wonderful — everything seems possible — and there's no need to spoil it with skepticism. Vermeulen and van den Akker name enthusiasm as one of the poles between which the feeling of our time oscillates. After a long era of postmodern irony, when delight seemed naive, metamodernism rehabilitates it: you can rejoice in earnest. At the same time, the metamodern person knows the pendulum swings, and the high will give way to something else. This knowledge doesn't cancel the joy but makes it gentler. From this point of view, you can fully live the euphoria while remembering that it is one phase of the oscillation, not a new permanent world. And when the wave settles, what may remain is the memory that the world is capable of being this open.
euphoria.practice: Describe in two or three words what exactly is bringing you joy right now. Keep this note — later it will remind you that such a feeling is possible.

crash.text: The drop after a high can be very hard — as if the world had suddenly faded. Many people know this feeling, and it is not your fault. Metamodernism describes our time through the image of a pendulum: feeling oscillates between enthusiasm and melancholy, hope and doubt. From this point of view, one could say that the comedown is not proof that the high was unreal, but the pendulum swinging the other way. Metamodernism does not treat melancholy as a mistake: it is just as legitimate a pole as joy. The main thing is to remember that the pendulum doesn't get stuck forever. Right now you don't have to demand that the brightness come back; you can simply live in this phase, knowing it will pass too.
crash.practice: Write: "Right now the pendulum is on the side of…" — and name the feeling. Add one thing that was with you both on the high and now.

quote.text: We must go forth and oscillate!
quote.author: Luke Turner

panic.text: Panic is very frightening: a wave of terror, as if your heart and breathing had stopped obeying you. You are not alone in this, and such a wave usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Metamodernism speaks of oscillation — a swinging between poles. From this point of view, one could say that panic is a wave that rises and inevitably falls, not a state that will last forever. Right now there's no need to analyze or understand anything — neither ironically nor seriously. Metamodernism values the simple and direct, and in a moment of panic the most direct thing is the body: the floor under your feet, your breath, the objects around you.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor and take a few breaths where the exhale is longer than the inhale. Name aloud five objects around you, one after another.

dread.text: Existential dread — "what's the point of it all," the sense of an abyss and of finitude — is one of the heaviest feelings, and there is a lot of honesty in it. Vermeulen and van den Akker describe the metamodern attitude to the big questions through Kant's "as if": we act as if the world had meaning and direction, even though we know we have no proof. This is not self-deception but a conscious choice to live in earnest. From this point of view, one could say that metamodernism does not abolish the abyss, but it doesn't fall into it either: it oscillates between doubt and hope and keeps building meaning. The answer to "what's the point" is not final — it is the one you choose to live out today.
dread.practice: Write down one thing you're willing to live for "as if" it had meaning — a person, a cause, something beautiful. Give it a minute today.

fomo.text: The feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives and you're not where you should be is very familiar to our time. Metamodernism sees in our era a return of romantic longing — a yearning for something greater, better, far away. The Romantics called it Sehnsucht, and Vermeulen and van den Akker note "neo-romantic" features in contemporary culture. From this point of view, one could say that the fear of missing out is romantic longing in the age of the feed. Metamodernism doesn't ask you to get rid of it, but offers oscillation: acknowledge the pull toward "there" and at the same time notice the value of "here." You can want something else without devaluing your own life.
fomo.practice: Write: "I'd like to be…" and next to it: "And here I have…". Let both lines be true.

sleepless.text: Insomnia and 3 a.m. thoughts are exhausting, and not being able to sleep is not your fault. At night the protective irony of the day usually weakens, and thoughts become bare and heavy. From a metamodern point of view, one could say that this is a "structure of feeling" shared by many people: you are not the only one lying awake thinking about life right now. Metamodernism doesn't require you to resolve every question in order to fall asleep. It accepts that some questions can be held open, swinging between anxiety and hope. The night doesn't owe you answers. You can put the search for meaning off until morning and simply let yourself lie there.
sleepless.practice: Write your thoughts on a sheet of paper and set it aside, saying: "I'll come back to this in the morning." Take a few slow exhales, feeling the weight of your body on the bed.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply, and that pain is legitimate: you trusted, and your trust was deceived. After something like this it's easy to decide that sincerity is naivety and to hide behind cynicism. Metamodernism knows this crossroads well: postmodern irony was, in large part, exactly that kind of defense. But the "New Sincerity" offers another path — "informed naivety": you know people can let you down, and you still don't give up your capacity to trust. From this point of view, one could say: your trust wasn't foolishness, it was courage. Betrayal speaks about another person's action, not about openness having been a mistake. You can acknowledge the pain fully without concluding that you can never trust anyone again.
betrayal.practice: Write: "I don't want to lose my capacity for…" — and finish the sentence. That is what's worth protecting no matter what.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is agonizing, and often behind it lies the fear of losing someone very dear. Postmodern culture taught us to hide such feelings behind irony: "I don't care," "I'm above it." Metamodernism suggests being more honest: acknowledge the jealousy without being ashamed of it and without letting it take control. From a metamodern point of view, one could say that jealousy is an oscillation between love and fear, trust and doubt. Both poles are real. You don't have to choose between "I simply love" and "I'm simply afraid" — you can acknowledge both. A sincere "I'm scared of losing you" is often closer to the truth than control or coldness.
jealousy.practice: Ask yourself: "If I said this without irony and without reproach, how would it sound?" Write that sentence down for yourself.

resentment.text: Old resentment is heavy, and it is understandable — you really were hurt. Metamodernism doesn't write about resentment directly, but in the light of its ideas one could say this. Vermeulen and van den Akker set "reconstruction" — an attempt to build something anew — against endless deconstruction: taking apart, exposing, looking for the catch. Resentment often resembles an endless deconstruction of a single situation: it gets taken apart again and again, turning up ever new evidence of injustice. Metamodernism doesn't demand that you forget or forgive. It only suggests that, alongside taking the past apart, you try to build something new — however small, however uncertain. The resentment can remain part of your story, but it doesn't have to be its only plot.
resentment.practice: Write down one thing you'd like to build or do in your life that has nothing to do with this resentment. Add one small step toward it.

heartbreak.text: A broken heart hurts almost physically, and that pain speaks of how much you invested. Metamodernism treats love without quotation marks. Michel Gondry's film Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, often cited as an example of the metamodern sensibility, is precisely about a broken heart: the characters erase their memories of each other, but in the end decide to try again, even though they already know it may hurt. That is "informed naivety": knowing the risk and still choosing openness. From this point of view, your pain is not proof that loving was foolish. It is part of what makes love real, and it doesn't cancel your ability to love again.
heartbreak.practice: Write down one memory of this relationship that you wouldn't want to erase, even if it hurts right now.

impostor.text: The fear of being found out at any moment is familiar to a great many people — even to those you admire. Metamodernism can offer support here. Vermeulen and van den Akker describe the metamodern attitude as an attempt made "in spite of inevitable failure": trying in earnest, knowing there will be no perfection. From this point of view, one could say that feeling like an impostor is a sign that you have taken something on seriously rather than hiding behind the irony of "I wasn't even trying." No one is ever fully "ready." The metamodern person admits to being a little naive and does it anyway. Your doubt doesn't cancel your work. You can doubt and keep going at the same time — metamodernism considers exactly that kind of oscillation normal.
impostor.practice: Write down one thing you took on seriously despite your doubts. Note what exactly you have already done in it.

self_hatred.text: The inner critic can sound very convincing, but its verdict is not the truth about you. David Foster Wallace, a forerunner of the "New Sincerity," wrote about how irony, which at first helped expose lies, over time becomes a trap: it devalues everything, including ourselves. From this point of view, one could say that the inner critic often speaks in the very language of this merciless irony: it mocks, devalues, leaves nothing alive. Metamodernism suggests stepping back from that voice and allowing yourself sincerity toward yourself — saying something warm about yourself, even if it seems naive. Such kindness to yourself is neither weakness nor self-deception, but a refusal to live in a cage of constant mockery.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one mocking phrase from your inner critic. Then, next to it, write one sincere, warm sentence about yourself, even if it seems naive.

quote.text: Irony has only emergency use. Carried over time, it is the voice of the trapped who have come to enjoy their cage.
quote.author: Lewis Hyde (quoted by David Foster Wallace)
quote.source: D. F. Wallace, "E Unibus Pluram: Television and U.S. Fiction" (1993)

helplessness.text: Feeling powerless to change anything is hard, and it often reflects real circumstances rather than any weakness of yours. Metamodernism knows this feeling well: our time is full of huge problems in the face of which a single person seems small. Vermeulen and van den Akker describe a response through "pragmatic idealism" and Kant's "as if": acting as if the world could become better, even without guarantees. From this point of view, one could say that helplessness and hope don't exclude each other — you can swing between them. You don't have to believe in success in order to take a small step. It's enough to act "as if."
helplessness.practice: Choose one tiny thing that is within your power today, and do it "as if" it mattered.

procrastination.text: When you can't get started, it is more often fear, fatigue, or the sense that everything has to be done perfectly than laziness. From a metamodern point of view, you might notice that putting things off is sometimes tied to an ironic defense: as long as I haven't started, no one can say I failed. Vermeulen and van den Akker describe the metamodern movement as an attempt made "in spite of inevitable failure." This means you can begin while accepting imperfection in advance. Metamodernism doesn't require confidence; it offers "informed naivety": knowing it will be hard and still taking the first small step. An imperfect beginning is better than a perfect plan that stays in your head — and it says nothing about your worth.
procrastination.practice: Do the smallest part of the task — one sentence, one email — deliberately imperfectly. Note that you have started.

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home — a move, emigration, losing familiar ground — is a real loss, and its weight is understandable. Vermeulen and van den Akker link the word "meta" to Plato's "metaxy" — "between." The metamodern person lives between poles: between past and future, irony and sincerity. From this point of view, one could say that living between two places, two languages, two cultures is not a failure or a flaw but a particular way of being. You can long for your old home and build a new one at the same time, without choosing one. Metamodernism doesn't require you to decide where you "really" are. You can be "in between" and find your own truth in that.
uprooted.practice: Write down one thing you love about the old place and one about the new. Let them exist side by side.

overload.text: Overload from the endless feed and informational noise is exhausting, and it is an understandable reaction, not a weakness of yours. In his essay on television, David Foster Wallace already wrote about how screen culture draws us in, while ironic watching from the sidelines becomes a habit. And in his speech "This Is Water" he said that what matters most is learning to choose what to pay attention to amid the endless stream. From this point of view, one could say that the feed is the water we swim in and hardly notice. Simply noticing it is already a first step toward freedom. You don't need to give up everything; you can choose a few things.
overload.practice: Close the feed for two minutes and ask yourself: "What do I actually want to pay attention to right now?" Write down the answer.

quote.text: The really important kind of freedom involves attention and awareness and discipline, and being able truly to care about other people and to sacrifice for them over and over in myriad petty, unsexy ways every day.
quote.author: David Foster Wallace

unreality.text: The feeling that nothing is quite real can be strange and unsettling, and it deserves gentle care. Postmodernism spoke a great deal about a world of simulations and copies, where it is hard to find anything "real." Metamodernism, as Vermeulen and van den Akker see it, responds with a renewed interest in depth, authenticity and the real — even while understanding that we can never finally arrive at them. From this point of view, one could say that the sense of unreality is familiar to many people in the age of screens. You can act "as if" reality is right beside you — and start with something simple: touch, sound, smell. Small anchors like these don't argue with the feeling; they gently bring you back into contact with what is near.
unreality.practice: Touch something with a clear texture and name three sensations: temperature, weight, surface. Tell yourself: "This is here."

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a precious feeling, and there's no need to cover it up with embarrassed irony. Vermeulen and van den Akker see a "neo-romantic" turn in contemporary culture: a return of interest in the sublime, in mystery, in a beauty larger than ourselves. The Romantics sought to see the infinite in the everyday, and metamodernism once again allows us to do so without being embarrassed by our naivety. From this point of view, your reverence is not sentimentality but openness to the fact that the world is bigger than any explanation. You can simply let yourself stand and look, without commenting. Metamodernism doesn't require you to explain this feeling, share it, or draw a conclusion from it: it is enough that it happened.
awe.practice: Stay with whatever filled you with awe for one more minute, without speaking and without taking a photo. Notice what is happening in your body.

relief.text: Relief is a quiet and important feeling, and you can let it be here fully. From a metamodern point of view, one could say that relief is the moment when the pendulum, long held toward anxiety or tension, finally lets go. Metamodernism describes life as oscillation, and relief is a natural part of that motion. There's no need to devalue it with irony like "don't celebrate too soon" or "this won't last." The "New Sincerity" allows you to say to yourself plainly: I feel better, and that's good. You can simply enjoy this moment without hurrying on to the next worry. Relief reminds you that hard phases are not forever, and you can keep that knowledge for the future too.
relief.practice: Take a slow exhale and say to yourself plainly, without irony: "I feel lighter." Notice where in your body you feel it.

calm.text: Calm is a precious state, and you don't have to earn it. Metamodernism is often described through oscillation and movement, but in the light of its ideas one could say that even a swinging pendulum has moments of balance. Postmodern culture often suspected simple states of being naive, while metamodernism gives them back their dignity: you can simply sit, drink tea, look out the window — and not consider it banal. The "New Sincerity" applies to calm too: you don't need to explain it, be ironic about it, or turn it into productivity. You can simply be in it while it lasts, without worrying that it will end: the pendulum will return to this place more than once.
calm.practice: Sit for a minute, noticing one simple thing that is pleasant right now — warmth, light, quiet. Don't explain it; just notice it.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is the joyful sense that something new has suddenly become possible. Metamodernism values it especially: Vermeulen and van den Akker name enthusiasm as one of the poles between which the feeling of our time oscillates, and Luke Turner's "Metamodernist Manifesto" speaks of "pragmatic romanticism." After an era when enthusiasm seemed naive, you can once again catch fire in earnest. From this point of view, inspiration is not a childish illusion but a chance to begin something, even knowing it won't all go perfectly. You can enjoy it now and take a first step while it's alive, without being ashamed of your passion. If the inspiration fades later, that too is part of the oscillation, not a sign that the idea was bad.
inspiration.practice: Write down the idea while it's fresh, in one or two sentences. Note one small step you could take as soon as tomorrow.

schadenfreude.text: Almost everyone knows schadenfreude, even though it's awkward to admit. The internet culture of recent decades is largely built on it: compilations of other people's failures, memes, mockery as a way of being "in the know." Postmodern irony made such mockery almost the norm. Metamodernism describes a turn in which this irony starts to feel cramped, and people once again dare to be sincere and compassionate — without giving up humor. From a metamodern point of view, one could say: there's no need to hide schadenfreude; it's worth acknowledging honestly. And then allowing yourself an "oscillation" — a swing toward the other pole: imagining what that person is going through right now. Laughter and compassion can exist side by side. You don't have to choose between them once and for all, but you can notice which way the pendulum is moving.
schadenfreude.practice: Admit to yourself: "Yes, I enjoyed that." Then ask: "And what is he or she feeling right now?" — and stay with the answer.

contempt.text: Contempt often works like armor: you look down on others, and nothing can touch you. David Foster Wallace, considered a forerunner of metamodernism, described in his essay "E Unibus Pluram" how irony and mocking superiority became a cultural means of self-protection: someone who ridicules everything can never be caught being vulnerable. He also observed that over time this stance turns into a trap. From a metamodern point of view, one could say that contempt is a relative of that irony: it lets you avoid feeling what lies beneath it — hurt, disappointment, fear. Metamodernism suggests not abandoning your critical eye, but swinging between it and sincere interest. The question "What did this person do to me?" is often more honest than "Why are they so pathetic?"
contempt.practice: In your mind, replace the phrase "They're pathetic" with "It hurt me that…". Finish the sentence.

disgust.text: Disgust can be aimed at people, at situations and at yourself — and in every case it is involuntary. Especially familiar to people today is disgust at themselves, often called "cringe": a burning embarrassment about your own sincerity, enthusiasm, things you said in the past. Metamodern culture works with this cringe a great deal: in its films and books the characters are awkward, touching, "too much" — and that is exactly why they are alive. From a metamodern point of view, one could say that disgust at your own sincerity is an echo of the ironic era, when feeling in earnest was considered ridiculous. Metamodernism offers "informed naivety": knowing how you look from outside and still not turning away from yourself. Awkward doesn't mean unworthy.
disgust.practice: Recall one of your "cringe" moments and tell yourself: "It was awkward — and it was real." Notice what has changed.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is born of hurt and injustice, and it has a right to exist. Culture is full of revenge stories — films and series where the wrongdoer gets what they deserve — and these plots draw us in because they promise to restore justice. Metamodernism describes the ability to live with big meanings "as if": to believe in a story while knowing it is a story. From this point of view, one could say that a revenge fantasy can be acknowledged as a fantasy — with all its force, but also with the understanding that life is more complicated than a script. "Informed naivety" here means honestly wanting justice while soberly remembering that revenge rarely brings the relief it promises. Beneath the fantasy there usually lies a simple need — for your pain to be acknowledged.
revenge.practice: Write down the revenge fantasy in full, like a scene from a film. Beneath it, one line: "What I really need is…".

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at the people close to you, which you feel ashamed of afterward, is a deeply human experience. Metamodernism describes the emotional life of our time as "oscillation" — a swinging between poles: hope and melancholy, enthusiasm and skepticism. From this point of view, one could say that closeness also works like a pendulum: tenderness and irritation take turns, and one doesn't cancel the other. In his speech "This Is Water," Wallace spoke of our "default setting" — the habit of seeing ourselves as the center of the world, which makes other people seem like obstacles. He was talking about irritation with strangers, but the same happens with those we love. Stepping out of that setting doesn't mean not being angry; it means giving the other person back their depth. Anger doesn't give you the right to wound, but it doesn't make you a bad person either.
anger_at_loved.practice: When things are quieter, imagine this person's day through their eyes: what were they carrying today? Stay with that for a minute.

ambivalence.text: Loving someone and not being able to stand them at the same time is hard, especially if it seems that feelings should be clear-cut. Metamodernism describes precisely a life "in between." Vermeulen and van den Akker use Plato's word "metaxy" — a state between opposites, where a person doesn't choose one pole but swings between them. For them this is not weakness but an honest form of contemporary sensibility: you can be naive and knowing, hopeful and melancholic, all at once. From this point of view, one could say that mixed feelings toward someone close are not a malfunction but the normal state of a living bond. You don't have to decide what you "really" feel. You can let the pendulum swing and notice which side outweighs the other at any given moment.
ambivalence.practice: Throughout the day, jot in the margin of a notebook: "right now, more love" or "right now, more can't-stand-it." Simply watch the pendulum.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, a parting, or even the death of a seriously ill loved one is a feeling people are often ashamed of. But it is very common. Metamodernism starts from the idea that contradictory feelings are normal: you can laugh and cry, grieve and breathe out, at the same time. From this point of view, one could say that relief does not cancel love. It speaks of the weight you were carrying — fear, caregiving, exhaustion. The metamodern "New Sincerity" suggests naming such a feeling plainly, without self-justification and without self-condemnation. You don't need to prove to yourself that you loved "correctly." You can simply acknowledge: I feel relief, and I loved. Both sentences are true at once.
guilty_relief.practice: Write two sentences side by side: "I feel relief" and "I loved / I love." Don't put a "but" between them — only an "and."

indifference.text: Sometimes something "should" move you, and it doesn't, and that feels awkward. Vermeulen and van den Akker describe metamodernism as an oscillation between many poles, including between empathy and apathy. From this point of view, one could say that indifference is not your final essence but one point on the pendulum's arc. Sometimes, after overload or long tension, it simply freezes at the pole of apathy. In "This Is Water," Wallace said that real freedom is the freedom to choose what you pay attention to. You can't choose a feeling, but you can choose your attention. There's no need to force yourself to empathize; you can only gently turn your gaze toward something and give a feeling the chance to come, if it wants to.
indifference.practice: Choose one small thing near you and look at it for a minute with full attention. Don't wait for a feeling — just look.

escape.text: The wish to drop everything and run away — from a job, a city, a role — is familiar to many. Metamodernism owes a great deal to German Romanticism, which called this longing for "somewhere out there" Sehnsucht — a yearning for the distant and the better. Vermeulen and van den Akker speak of the "neo-romanticism" of our time: we know there is no perfect place, and we dream of it anyway. From this point of view, one could say that the dream of escape is neither naive nor foolish — it is a romantic desire that can be lived "as if": seriously imagining a different life while remembering that it too would be imperfect. Such a dream can tell you a lot about what is missing here. You don't need to decide anything big — it's enough to listen.
escape.practice: Describe in three sentences a day in the life you'd like to escape to. Note one detail you could add to today.

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone unavailable, or the "wrong" person, can be confusing and frightening. Metamodernism takes a great deal from the Romantics, and the Romantics knew this feeling better than anyone. Novalis has a symbol — the "blue flower," an image of endless longing for what can never be fully attained. Vermeulen and van den Akker describe the metamodern sensibility as a striving for the unattainable that knows it is unattainable. From this point of view, one could say that attraction to the unavailable often speaks of a longing for something bigger than the particular person: for a different life, for aliveness, for a different self. The attraction itself calls for neither condemnation nor action. You can approach it with "informed naivety": acknowledge its power and look with curiosity at what it's about.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Finish the sentence: "With this person, I could be…". Look at what this sentence says about your life.

social_anxiety.text: The fear of people and of being judged is agonizing: it seems everyone notices your every awkward moment. In his essay "E Unibus Pluram," Wallace wrote that television culture made us hyper-self-conscious: we are so used to watching others that we constantly see ourselves through the eyes of an imagined viewer. From this point of view, one could say that social anxiety is largely an effect of this inner screen, not the truth about how others perceive you. Metamodernism offers "informed naivety": knowing that you may look awkward from outside — and still taking part, speaking, trying. It is precisely awkward sincerity, in Wallace's view, that makes a person alive. Others, most likely, are busy with their own inner screens too.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a meeting, tell yourself: "I may look awkward — and still be here." Take one small step toward others.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is hard: you want guarantees, and there aren't any. Metamodernism offers a particular stance for this. Drawing on Kant, Vermeulen and van den Akker speak of living "as if": acting as if the goal were achievable, even without being sure that it is. They call this stance "pragmatic idealism." Their "Notes on Metamodernism" contains the thought that metamodernism moves forward even though it knows the truth may never be found. From this point of view, one could say that uncertainty requires neither blind faith nor despair. You can hold both doubt and hope in mind at the same time, and take the next step without knowing the whole road.
uncertainty.practice: Finish the sentence: "I will act as if…". Choose one small action in that spirit for today.

waiting.text: Waiting — for an answer, for results, for news — leaves you suspended, where neither hope nor fear can win. Metamodernism knows this "in between" well. Vermeulen and van den Akker use Plato's word "metaxy" — dwelling between two poles — as the key to contemporary sensibility. From this point of view, one could say that waiting is not empty time but a particular state in which the pendulum swings between "everything will be fine" and "everything is bad." Fighting this swinging is pointless; you can simply notice its rhythm, the way you notice your breathing. And allow yourself to live in the gaps: drink tea, talk to someone, look out the window. The pendulum's swinging doesn't cancel the fact that you are here.
waiting.practice: Set a timer for five minutes and do something simple with your hands. When it goes off, notice which way the pendulum has swung.

regret.text: Regret over something done or left undone can hold on for a long time. Metamodernism describes a time when people once again take their own history seriously, after an era in which the past was often turned into a game of quotations. From this point of view, one could say that regret is worth living through sincerely, without hiding behind the irony of "oh well, whatever." But metamodernism also offers the other pole — sobriety: back then you knew less than you know now, and you acted within those circumstances. And the "as if" stance lets you look forward: act as if something could still be done differently — because often it really can. Swinging between pain about the past and hope for the future is not inconsistency but a living form of growing up.
regret.practice: Write: "I regret that…", and below it: "As if it were still possible, I could…". Notice what resonated.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person aches quietly and stubbornly. In an ironic culture such feelings were often hidden, as though longing were a little shameful. The metamodern "New Sincerity" gives them back their voice: you can simply tell yourself "I miss them" — without a smirk, without caveats. Vermeulen and van den Akker write that the metamodern sensibility oscillates between hope and melancholy. From this point of view, one could say that longing, too, swings between these poles: at times you want them back, at times a gentle acceptance comes. You don't have to stop the pendulum. Longing tells you that this person held a real place in your life, and acknowledging that is already a form of respect — for yourself and for them.
longing.practice: Write this person a letter you won't send. In it, simply say honestly what you miss.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — over wars, disasters, injustice — can be almost unbearable. Vermeulen and van den Akker linked the emergence of the metamodern sensibility to the series of crises at the start of the century: financial, ecological, social. At such a time irony stops saving us, and people once again want to believe the world can become better — while knowing how hard that is. They call this stance "pragmatic idealism." From this point of view, one could say that there's no need to be ashamed of your pain, and no need to drown in it. You can swing between grief and hope, allowing yourself both to weep for the world and to do something small in it. Hope here is not naivety but a decision to act "as if" change were possible.
world_pain.practice: Limit your time with the news and choose one small thing that will make the world a little gentler today — even if it's right next to you.

rejection.text: Rejection hurts, and it hurts especially if you opened up sincerely. Irony long served as insurance: if you spoke about your feelings with a smirk, you couldn't truly be rejected. Wallace suggested that the new rebels would be those who dared to speak in earnest, risking mockery and condescending smiles. Metamodernism describes this as the "New Sincerity" — a willingness to risk looking naive. From this point of view, one could say that rejection is the price of sincerity, not proof that sincerity was a mistake. You did what many don't dare to do: you opened up without armor. It hurts, but it also speaks of your courage. The refusal belongs to this one encounter, not to your right to feel.
rejection.practice: Write: "I took a risk and opened up." Read it as an acknowledgment of courage, not of a mistake.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned can sit deep and surface even on calm days. There is nothing shameful in it. Metamodernism speaks of a "structure of feeling" — the shared emotional climate of an era. Today's climate is shaped largely by instability and the sense that anything can change at any moment: jobs, places, relationships. From this point of view, one could say that your fear is not only a personal story but also a response to that shared climate. And the metamodern "as if" stance offers a gentle way of living with it: trusting "as if" the bond is reliable, without demanding absolute guarantees from it. This is not naivety but "informed naivety": you know the risks — and you still choose trust.
abandonment.practice: Recall a time when someone stayed by your side even though they could have left. Write it down and reread it when the fear comes back.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love combines the strength of a feeling with its impossibility — and that is exhausting. Vermeulen and van den Akker wrote that metamodernism attempts in spite of inevitable failure and seeks what it may never find. The formula sounds almost like a description of unrequited love. From this point of view, one could say there is nothing foolish in your feeling: it is one of the most romantic, most "metamodern" forms of sincerity — to love in earnest without guarantees. But metamodernism is also oscillation: beside the pole of hope there is the pole of sobriety. You can respect your feeling and at the same time, gradually, let it grow quieter. Love without return does not diminish your capacity to love.
unrequited.practice: Write down what you respect yourself for in this love. Separately, write one thing that today belongs only to you.

humiliation.text: Humiliation wounds deeply: someone tried to make you look ridiculous or worthless. You have a right to this pain. Ironic culture turned mockery into a weapon: to ridicule is to be above. In his essay "E Unibus Pluram," Wallace wrote that the new rebels would have to risk yawns, rolled eyes, cool smiles and cries of "Oh how banal." He saw the willingness to withstand mockery not as a disgrace but as courage. From a metamodern point of view, one could say that humiliation says more about those who use mockery as armor than about you. Your sincerity, your feelings and your dignity are not made smaller because someone laughed at them. Sometimes what gets ridiculed turns out to be the most alive.
humiliation.practice: Write down what about you someone tried to ridicule. Below it, write why it is valuable to you.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body is very common, and there's nothing to be ashamed of in it. Postmodern culture is often described as a culture of surfaces and images, where everything turns into a picture. The social media feed is its direct heir: bodies get compared with retouched images. Metamodernism describes a desire to bring back depth — what lies behind the picture. From this point of view, one could say that your body is not an image but the place where you live, feel, embrace, get tired. "Informed naivety" lets you know about beauty standards and still treat your body with sincere warmth — not because it measures up, but because it is yours. You can swing between criticism and tenderness, but give tenderness a little more room.
body_shame.practice: Name one part of your body and one thing it does for you. Say "thank you" to it — in earnest, without irony.

illness.text: Illness, when your body lets you down, takes away your strength and your familiar rhythm — that is hard, and you have every right to be sad and angry. Metamodernism speaks of oscillation between hope and melancholy, and in illness this pendulum is especially noticeable: today it seems everything will be all right, tomorrow that there's no strength left. From this point of view, one could say that this swinging is normal and doesn't need fixing. In "This Is Water," Wallace said that even amid tedious, difficult everyday life you can choose what to pay attention to. That doesn't cancel the pain or require you to be cheerful. But sometimes attention to something small — a warm cup, light, the voice of someone close — gives you something to hold on to when the bigger supports are temporarily out of reach.
illness.practice: Find one small pleasant thing in this day — a taste, a sound, some light. Let your attention rest on it for a minute.

pride.text: Pride in something you've done is a good, well-earned feeling. In ironic culture it was often hidden: being proud in earnest seemed immodest or ridiculous, so achievements were customarily played down with a joke. The metamodern "New Sincerity" gives back the right to rejoice in your work openly. From this point of view, one could say that telling yourself "I did this, and it's good" is not bragging but honesty. At the same time, metamodernism keeps the oscillation: you can be proud while also remembering the doubts, the difficulties, the help of others. Such pride is not arrogant and belittles no one: it is warm, rather like gratitude to yourself for persevering. Let yourself enjoy it without rushing to add "oh, it's nothing."
pride.practice: Say aloud: "I did this." Don't add irony or caveats — just stay with those words for a moment.

melancholy.text: Bright sadness is one of the most metamodern of feelings. Vermeulen and van den Akker describe our era as an oscillation between hope and melancholy, and many metamodern films and songs live in exactly this tone: sad, but warm. Metamodernism is heir to the Romantics, for whom melancholy was not an illness but a sensitivity to the infinite showing through the everyday. Novalis called on us to "romanticize" the world — to give the familiar a sense of mystery. From this point of view, one could say that your bright sadness is a way of seeing the world more deeply: noticing that everything passes, and so becomes more precious. You don't need to climb out of it; you can savor it, like good music at dusk.
melancholy.practice: Put on a song that captures this mood exactly, and listen to it all the way through, doing nothing else.
